#4353. 10 Deltarune Moments That Feel Totally Different When You Replay Earlier Chapters

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Deltarune is a game that thrives not only on its narrative, but also on the individual mysteries set up by every cliffhanger and loose thread. As in any good story, major revelations have not only affected fans’ expectations for the future, but also their understanding of earlier events.

Thanks to fantastic use of irony and follow-through, some of the smallest moments in Deltarune’s earlier chapters have been completely recontextualized, and we’ll be talking about the wildest here.

As we wait for chapter 6, it’s important to lay out everything we know and everything that’s become clearer since the game’s initial demo release. They say hindsight is 20/20, so let’s see how it serves us going forward.

Ralsei’s recitation of the Prophecy is one of the first major setup moments in Deltarune, both as a fairly cliché story setup and a direct threat for the party to fight back against later. Since chapter 4, the Prophecy’s legitimacy and exact wording have been under heavy scrutiny.

Knowing that Ralsei knows everything destined to happen down to the minute details makes his narration and people-pleasing more unsettling than charming. Susie’s heavy relevance to the darkest parts of its story sets her romantic yearning for Noelle up as a major red flag, ripe for getting ripped down by the grimmer chapters to come.

Susie’s portion of the Prophecy is vague enough that it might not even be about her, whether that’s through a misstep by Ralsei or deliberate sabotage from an outside force. The Prophecy itself is far from set in stone, ironically, and subverting it is already becoming a major objective of the party.

This is a detailed and all purpose hub for Toby Fox's episodic Deltarune.

Throughout King’s fight at the tail end of the chapter, he spends most of his dialogue praising the Roaring Knight, assigning all his work and progress to their support. This was the very first mention we got of the Knight, and at the time most assumed they were some kind of fixture of the card kingdom.

We’ve gathered much more info on the Roaring Knight since, but King’s speech is the only case we have of them actually interacting with someone without hostility.

In every other appearance, they’ve been a snarling aggressor with cruel laughter as their only method of communication. Hearing that they not only aligned with King but inspired him does a lot for their threat, establishing them as more than just a beast.

The weird route was already unsettling enough when it dropped during Deltarune’s second chapter, adding a touch of that No Mercy dread Undertale was infamous for. Despite this, the route felt rather self-contained until chapter 4 gave players a chance to lock it in.

Now that chapter 5 has arrived and given us a massive follow-through, playing through chapter 2’s Weird Route feels even worse. Knowing how far it goes and seeing exactly what goes on to shatter Noelle’s psyche make the metanarrative pain hit all the harder.

Spamton’s Shadow Crystal fight is a massive tonal shift from the rest of the chapter on the main route, especially at the very end. The battle takes a lot of notes from Undertale’s Mettaton battles, with Spamton straight up taking on a form extremely similar to Mettaton NEO.

The actual text of the battle is all about Spamton trying to transcend his limits, which all sounds very familiar to anyone who has seen chapter 5’s Weird Route dialogue. Combined with the constant discussion of Heaven and his angelic design, Spamton’s fight feels very different from what we originally thought.

Angels specifically are feeling more and more relevant the longer the game goes, both to symbolize the player and the larger figures controlling the Prophecy. For a goofy salesman, Spamton feels far more relevant than ever expected.

As Deltarune's size and popularity only grows, many people wonder if they should play Undertale first, and they really should.

The Shelter, the massive bunker at the southernmost tip of Hometown’s map, has been mysterious since Deltarune’s very first chapter, with each release slowly giving us more and more details about it. Over time, we’ve learned plenty. It is likely the site of whatever terrible accident happened to Dess; multiple members of the town are acting to keep it sealed, and most recently, Kris has access to it.

Thanks to these facts, it is largely assumed to be some kind of central base for the Knight and whoever is assisting it in the Light World. This makes Kris’s access to it when they break our control all the more interesting. Kris is clearly willing to do something drastic, including working with those who directly oppose the party.

After the most recent reveal of the strange flower seeds Kris pocketed and likely took back to the bunker, it feels like we’re watching them teetering over a ledge with no way to help. If they’d even let us.

Tenna is a massive source of comedy in chapter 3, but he’s also the source of a very off-putting little tantrum towards the tail end of the chapter, right before his boss fight. In it, he laments not only the state of the Dreemurr family but specifically Kris, pointing out just how differently they’ve been acting over the course of the night.

We know that the source of this difference is the player’s interference, but that dichotomy is a major stress point, both for Kris and the player. Who knows what Kris really acts like and whether or not close friends like Susie, who met them after the swap, will actually care about them?

On our end, we really don’t know what Kris is capable of or what they’re willing to do when the chips are down, and it adds a layer of dread to the entire scene.

From Cooking, to the Rhythm game, and even Susiezilla, this is How To S-Rank All Minigames in Deltarune Chapter 3.

After all the buildup and vague hints towards the Knight, their sudden reveal in chapter 3 was a massive surprise, and the small amount of characterization we’ve gotten for them has painted a picture of their true motives.

Most interestingly, the scene that plays when you beat the Knight, where they seemingly knight Kris, has been given extra weight by how clearly Kris is standing in their corner. After fighting off the Flowers and pocketing the highly toxic seeds at the tail end of chapter 5, Kris is willing to go above and beyond, even considering harming themselves to align with the Knight’s goal.

This is a horrifying setup for what chapters 6 and 7 could bring, especially with 5 being marketed as “one last happy adventure.”

Working your way through Noelle’s house at the start of chapter 4 was a great peek into her psyche after not getting much for her in chapter 3, while also allowing us to put together a bit more info on Dess Holiday herself.

Not only did we get plenty of extra scenes between Susie and Noelle, but we also got some more direct moments to see how exactly Kris acts without the Soul piloting them, making it clear that they can survive without it, at least for limited periods.

Most importantly, finally meeting Hometown’s mayor, Carol Holiday, added a tension that immediately made her a candidate for the Knight to many players. I won’t say I fully buy that theory, but she is officially on the table as an incredibly potent threat, alluding to both knowledge of and cooperation with Kris’s goal.

Chapter 4’s dark world was shockingly somber at times, setting a future tone while finalizing quite a few rules for how light world monsters and Darkners can overlap. Namely, through Gerson’s inclusion, we learned that dead Darkners, at least monsters, can manifest in Dark Worlds if items with their dust are within a fountain’s range.

This opens the door for any missing or dead characters to potentially show up in the future, or for items connected deeply to certain characters to manifest either as them or similarly to them. I fully believe this is how we’ll get some extra context on Rudy after his “falling down” early in chapter 5, and that it will lead to massive drama going forward.

From the earliest launch of Deltarune, fans have assumed the strange voice that speaks to us during the character creator was Gaster, based on the speech pattern that it uses and the dialogue from the Deltarune Twitter.

Following his extra dialogue in chapters 3 and 4, I grew extremely confident in that theory, and facts from both the normal and Weird Routes of chapter 5 have fully convinced me that we will meet the Man Who Speaks in Hands before Deltarune is through. Given what happens to Onionsan via one of Gaster’s Goners and his clear significance in the “B-Side” cutscene in the Weird Route, he is by far our biggest mystery and one that fully recontextualizes every bit of dialogue we get from him.

Deltarune chapter 5 is, unsurprisingly, full of mysteries players are still trying to get their heads around.

#4352. Volkswagen may have just hinted at the name of its next affordable EV

Volkswagen is getting ready to launch a new electric car starting at about €20,000 ($22,000) in 2027, and it looks like the entry-level EV may no longer be nameless. A newly filed trademark could have just given away what VW plans to call it.

The new entry-level EV is “the last piece of the puzzle,” Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said last March after unveiling the ID. EVERY1 concept car.

Volkswagen said the production version will launch in 2027 with a starting price of around €20,000 ($22,000).

The new model will sit below the ID. Polo in Volkswagen’s Electric Urban Car Family, a lineup of compact, affordable electric cars.

Volkswagen’s current entry-level EV lineup includes the ID. Polo, ID. Cross, the Cupra Raval, and Skoda Epiq, all based on its new MEB+ platform.

After launching the lower-priced standard versions of the ID. Polo and ID. Cross recently, starting at €24,995 and €27,995, respectively, Volkswagen is preparing to launch an even smaller, more affordable EV next year.

A recent trademark filing with the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) and the German DPMA may have just revealed the name of VW’s upcoming €20,000 EV.

Volkswagen filed a trademark application for the name ID. UP on October 22, 2026, with the EUIPO and DPMA, suggesting this will be the name of the upcoming electric car in 2027.

The trademark follows previous reports that VW planned to revive the former Up! name as part of its shift away from its previous numerical naming scheme (ID.3, ID.4, ID.5, etc.).

Volkswagen has kept most details a secret thus far. Like the ID. Polo, the first to go on sale with an established VW nameplate, the ID. UP is expected to use the same 37 kWh LFP battery to reduce costs.

The VW ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery offers a WLTP range of up to 334 km (207 miles), so the smaller ID. UP will likely provide around the same, if not slightly more.

Volkswagen said it will offer at least 250 km (155 miles) of range. It will also use a new 70 kW (94 hp) electric motor, enabling a top speed of 130 km/h (80 mph).

The production version of the ID. EVERY1, expected to arrive as the ID. UP, will be one of nine new models VW plans to launch by 2027.

Volkswagen previously said the entry-level EV will be 3,880 mm long, which would position it between the former Up! (3,600 mm) and the ID. Polo (4,053 mm). Despite its compact size, VW said the electric city car will seat four passengers and offer a luggage compartment volume of 305 liters.

The VW Group’s new Electric Urban Car Family is off to a strong start, securing nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June.

All models within the family are built on the MEB+ platform with a FWD powertrain, and share more than 80% of the components and tech.

Volkswagen said the production version of the ID. EVERY1 will be among the first vehicles based on its zonal, software-defined vehicle (SDV) architecture, which it is developing through its joint venture with Rivian.

Ah, finally a car in the upper range of being meaningful and sensible.

If someone needs more, then those are obviously special needs people. Being like can't enter and exit such a sensible car. Or like having to move the 15 horses of their 5 daughters. Or being a fieldworker driving a gazillion miles every day. Or requiring a lot of attention from lesser beings.

In March, the Rivian and Volkswagen Group Technologies (RV Tech) joint venture tested the new SDV architecture on the ID. EVERY1, alongside Audi and Scout reference vehicles, validating over-the-air (OTA) capabilities.

The new architecture will enable “highly automated driving features” and “advanced infotainment solutions,” with continuous OTA updates.

While VW said it will deploy the SDV architecture in “electric vehicles across markets in the Western Hemisphere,” the entry-level EV is not expected to reach the States.

Volkswagen is, however, preparing to launch the ID. Tiguan, which will launch in 2027 as the successor to the ID.4 (and ID.5 in Europe).

#4350. Honkai: Star Rail 3.8 will run for an extra two weeks while Version 4.0 is in the oven

The next Honkai: Star Rail update is upon us, and there's a mix of good - and unusual news.

HoYoverse just hosted a sizeable Honkai: Star Rail Special Program, revealing more than just the game’s next major update. Version 3.8 was the big highlight, of course, with the new release arriving soon, on December 16-17 depending on your server region.

Alongside showing everything coming with this next update, the developer also announced that 3.8 will go on for eight weeks, rather than the usual six. V3.8 is dubbed "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams", and it brings an end to the Amphoreus journey.

The story in "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams" takes place after the final battle of Amphoreus, where Constance "The Dahlia" appears to deliver a twist: the Trailblazer's memories are scattered, with many parts missing.

This final quest revolves around finding them in order to piece together the mystery, and involves a return to Penacony. This memory-hunting adventure is told from the perspective of Firefly, which will also explain how she entered the dreamscape initially and met the squad.

The new playable character is The Dahlia, whose power is linked to the the Remembrance path, which allows her to fabricate memories. Despite taking her powers from the Remembrance, The Dhalia actually follows the Path of Nihility in-game: she’s a 5-Star character who shines in teams dealing Break DMG.

The Dhalia can unleash a Gloomy Zone that causes Toughness Reduction inflicted by allies to trigger Super Break DMG, even before you break your enemies’ Weaknesses. The Dahlia can also invite one teammate to become her Dance Partner, which allows them (and her) to deal additional Super Break DMG each time they attack an enemy. If you trigger her Ultimate after picking a Dance Partner, she applies Type Weaknesses of both partners to enemies.

While The Dahlia is the only new character appearing in this final Amphoreus update, there'll be reruns aplenty, with an unusual third banner phase to make up for the extra long wait for 4.0. Appropriately for her role in the story, Firefly will make her return alongside The Dahlia in Phase 1, while Fugue and Lingsha will both have banner reruns in Phase 2, which is expected on January 7th. A bonus two-week-long Phase 3 will then begin on January 28th, seeing brief reappearances for popular returning characters Aglaea and Sunday, before things (presumably) go back to normal with the new annual update.

Something else to look forward to in 3.8 is The Chrysos Awoo Championship, which invites players to become chimera trainers and compete in team-based battles. The Remnants of Twilight event kicks off with the new patch, too, featuring its own set of challenges. However, HoYoverse have confirmed that there won't be an extra event during Phase 3 — but hopefully that'll give you some time to wrap up the last of the Amphoreus story content, which is longer than the previous four chapters put together.

#4349. Rinnai’s new heat pump water heaters get smarter – and easier to install

Rinnai has launched a new lineup of electric heat pump water heaters that adds wifi controls and more installation options to an appliance that can cut the energy needed for hot showers.

The REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes. It builds on Rinnai’s existing REHP lineup, with changes designed to make the units easier to install, monitor, and maintain.

Heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank. Moving that heat requires less electricity than producing it with conventional electric resistance elements. There’s no fuel combustion at the appliance, although emissions from its electricity supply depend on the grid.

Rinnai lists a Uniform Energy Factor, or UEF, of 3.75 for the 50-gallon model and 4.0 for the two larger versions. Higher numbers mean greater efficiency under standardized testing; actual bills depend on electricity rates, hot water use, and installation conditions.

The lineup delivers up to 91 gallons of hot water in the first hour, depending on tank size. That rating includes both stored hot water and what the unit can heat during that hour – useful context when several people take consecutive showers.

There are five operating modes, 4.5 kW backup heating elements, and a variable-speed fan designed to keep noise down. The heat pump can operate with ambient air as low as 37°F.

Installation is where some of the more practical upgrades show up.

The new Rinnai heat pump water heater units have water connections on both the top and side, giving installers more options for connecting existing plumbing. Both the air intake and exhaust are on top, allowing zero side clearance where Rinnai’s installation requirements permit.

An optional ducting kit adds flexibility for tighter spaces. Carrying handles help with moving the tank into place, and the air filter slides out horizontally from the side for cleaning.

Rinnai has also added a third tank temperature sensor to the 50- and 80-gallon models to help manage hot water delivery.

Wifi adds remote monitoring and control. Rinnai’s updated Central app supports the REHPW series, including scheduling and tools to use time-of-use electricity rates to manage energy use.

The units also carry CTA-2045 AC Level 2 certification for demand response. That gives compatible utility programs a way to communicate with the water heater and adjust its electricity use. Rinnai says the certification can help qualify homeowners for local and state utility demand-response rebates; availability depends on the program.

The series is Energy Star certified, meets NEEA Tier 4 requirements, and complies with California’s Title 24 requirements, including JA13, according to Rinnai. Warranty coverage includes 10 years for the tank and other parts, plus one year for labor.

I’m very happy with my hybrid heat pump water heater. I run it in heat pump only mode in summer and it helps cool the house for free. For anyone on the fence, especially your utility offers a rebate, it’s definitely worth looking at.

Rinnai directs buyers to an installer for pricing, so the upfront cost – and how much a local rebate might offset it – will require a quote. However, the REHP series price on Amazon hovers around the $2,000 mark.

#4348. Tesla Cybercab orders open at $29,990 + $299/mo, only in Robotaxi zones

Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”

And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.

The order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.

The subscription isn’t optional. It’s pre-checked on the order page at $299 per month, with one month included, and the fine print says “Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate.”

The email is even more direct. Its asterisk reads: “Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation.”

The rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and says you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”

Musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

Tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.

And those service areas aren’t what Tesla says they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.

Railroad crossings are a big reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.

Then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential. NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.

I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.

Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.

Sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

No point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).

And here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” currently around Q2 2027, while asking people to buy a new two-seater that can do nothing else.

If the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla says it does?

Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.

See all results for new 2027 Acura Integra Type S for sale near 29405

The Acura Integra Type S is the swankier cousin of the boy-racer Honda Civic Type R. The two share their mechanical underpinnings and hatchback body style, but the Acura is dressed in a more respectable-looking outfit. A lusty 320-hp turbocharged inline-four is under the hood and mates exclusively to a six-speed manual transmission. The combination loves to spin its front tires excitedly, and it's a riot to drive.

An expertly tuned chassis gives the Integra Type S high-spirited handling, and it rides comfortably enough for long trips. The engineers responsible for this gem had driving enthusiasts in mind when this Acura was planned. The cabin is slightly upscale from the Civic Type-R as well, although not as much as you’d think given the six grand price delta between the two.

Expert Tip: Its premium badge and $ 56,000 price tag put the Integra Type S into contention with some European rivals that offer richer accommodations.

Compare the 2027 Acura Integra Type S with the top vehicles in this segment with our new compare tool.

Acura has added a limited-production Heritage Edition to the lineup for 2027. Only 700 will be offered in the U.S., all painted Blazing Phoenix Yellow and wearing special copper-colored aluminum wheels. The Heritage Edition is also emblazoned with black exterior badging and features a titanium shift knob.

The standard Integra Type S gets a few changes for the 2027 model year, too, including new gloss black wheels, yellow brake calipers, dark gray interior trim, and gloss black climate control knobs. Several features have been added as standard, such as memory settings for the driver’s seat and an exterior mirror tilt-down feature that can be set to automatically dip the mirrors when you shift into reverse.

If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.

A 320-hp turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four with 310 pound-feet of torque is the sole engine for the Integra Type S. Like the Civic Type R, the Integra Type S routes the power exclusively through a six-speed manual transmission and front-wheel drive with a limited-slip differential. Shifter action is wonderfully light and precise—this is one of the best manual shifters in the business—and clutch take-up is smooth and intuitive. With all 310 pound-feet of torque available at 2600 rpm, you could skip a shift or two without worry, but it'd be a shame to miss out on all the fun.

Objectively, roadholding and braking match the Civic Type R, with the Integra Type S pulling 1.02 g's on the skid pad and stopping from 70 mph in just 153 feet. Subjectively, the Civic feels ever so slightly more vivacious from behind the wheel. The Integra Type S knows how to chill in less demanding situations, slipping into an almost-calm cruising mode. All Type S models come with 19-inch wheels wearing summer tires, Brembo brakes, and an exhaust system with three center-mounted exhaust pipes.

Car and Driver calculates your car's value in three free and easy steps - using the same Black Book® data dealers use to appraise vehicles.

In Comparison: The Integra Type S's brisk 60-mph sprint time is nearly two seconds quicker than the 7.0-second time we posted with the standard six-speed Integra and just 0.2 seconds behind the last Civic Type R we tested.

The EPA estimates that the Integra Type S will deliver 21 mpg city, 28 mpg highway, and 24 mpg combined. It's also worth noting the Type S returned an impressive 31 mpg on our 75-mph highway fuel-economy test, three miles per gallon better than its EPA rating. For more information about the Integra Type S's fuel economy, visit the EPA's website.

In Comparison: The Audi S3 is slightly more efficient, earning EPA estimates of 23 mpg city and 31 mpg highway, as is the BMW M235 Gran Coupe with estimates of 24 mpg city and 33 mpg highway.

First Row: Acura plays the long game with the Type S's interior, favoring conservative design and quality materials over outright flash. There are plenty of parts shared with the Honda Civic under the skin, but Acura pulls styling elements from its SUVs to foster the familial vibe. Distinctive features include mildly bolstered sport seats upholstered with perforated, faux-suede fabric, “Type S” embossed headrests, and subtle touches including a Type S shift knob, boot, and steering wheel emblem.

Second Row: A pair of individual rear bucket seats and a small center console armrest replace the standard Integra's rear bench. There's room for two in back, but the lack of features such as rear air vents and seat heaters is a notable omission in a supposedly premium car.

Cargo Capacity: Thanks to its Civic roots, the Integra Type S offers the same 24 cubic feet of cargo room accessed via a large hatchback. We fit five carry-on suitcases in the trunk and managed to squeeze in a total of 18 with the rear seats folded.

The Type S gets the same 10.2-inch digital gauge cluster as the rest of the Integra lineup; a 9.0-inch infotainment touchscreen is standard. A wireless smartphone charging pad, a head-up display, and a pair of USB ports are also included. All versions come with a top-tier 16-speaker, 530-watt ELS Studio 3D premium audio system.

A host of driver-assistance features are included as standard in the Integra Type S, including automated emergency braking with pedestrian detection, lane-keeping assist, and adaptive cruise control.

For information about the Integra Type S's crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.

Acura offers a longer powertrain warranty than most of its competitors, with powertrain coverage stretching up to six years or 70,000 miles. Complimentary scheduled maintenance is also included, unlike the Audi S3 or the Mercedes-Benz CLA-Class.

#4346. Tomorrow’s Battlefield 6 patch is the first step towards improving footstep audio, and it might actually fix the settings reset bug

The next major Battlefield 6 patch is nearly upon us, and Battlefield Studios is promising a bounty of changes - including a couple of fixes to some big bugs.

Battlefield 6 is about to receive a new update. Version 1.1.3.0 is set to arrive tomorrow, December 9 to kick off the third and final phase of the game’s first season. Winter Offensive brings some holiday-themed new content to the game, but it’s not the most interesting part of the patch.

That honour goes to a couple of the high-level changes Battlefield Studios has included with the new patch, which range from a major pass on audio to a fix for a particularly annoying bug that’s been seemingly introduced with a recent patch.

Thew new content takes the form of a limited-time version of the game’s Empire State map, which covers it in snow and tweaks its layout slightly. To go along with that there are new limited-time modes for both multiplayer and Redsec’s Gauntlet. The event mode will be available in Conquest, and Domination.

The Ice Climbing Axe is the only new weapon in this drop. The battle pass gets a new Winter Offensive bonus path, just like we’ve seen with previous seasonal stages. This is how you unlock the axe, too.

Easily the most interesting change in this update is the range of improvements to audio across the board. First, footstep audio received a big pass that should make it easier to hear enemy footsteps, easier to locate them, and across different surfaces.

Some of the bugs that caused certain sounds to simply vanish have been fixed. This was especially prevalent in battle royale matches. BF Studios explained in the patch notes that it has adjusted memory priorities for in-game sounds in order to prioritise the most crucial ones. This is not the end of the road on audio, however, as the developer continues to work on making the soundscape more stable and reliable.

Some of those audio changes are the result of recent testing done in Battlefield Labs, which is also responsible for another exciting addition in this latest patch: improvements to hit registration.

While BF6 has had solid and stable netcode, certain situations would sometimes create uncertainty about how you died, and why certain actions seemingly failed to perform at that particular moment.

The focus in this update is to improve the reliability of how actions in close-quarter combat are translated, which includes firing before fully going into ADS, quick aim changes and more.

Speaking of close-range, the patch also brings another pass to soldier visibility to make it easier for enemies to stand out from the background. This is particularly relevant in areas with low contrast, or busy environments with lots of particle and visual effects.

1.1.3.0 also brings yet another set of weapon handling and gunplay tweaks, this time focusing on accuracy issues with first shots. You can also expect more tweaks to attachment behaviour with regards to recoil.

Something else worth highlighting is that vehicle gameplay is getting several smaller tweaks that have to do with how they interact with the world, how their HUDs behave and more. Finally, your settings should no longer be reset after applying an update. BF Studios says there are still some instances where that might happen, but the issue should be fixed for the majority of players.

You can read the full change log on the Battlefield blog.

#4345. 10 Open-World Games You Can Finish in 10 Hours & Under

Elena Chapella is a Writer for DualShockers. Previously an award-winning journalist, Elena is passionate about writing what she loves.

When any gamer hears about open world games, they immediately (safely) assume that the game would proceed to take hours upon hours to complete. However, that’s not always the case with open world games.

In fact, some of these games can be completed in less than 10 hours.

If you enjoy exploration-focused titles that are free of filler, we recommend the ten fastest open-world games to 100%.

For players who are wanting a one-and-done experience with an open world game, being able to beat it within the same day or two days maximum, these games scratch that itch. You’re able to hop in and complete the game practically quicker than you can download it, and it’s just the right amount of content to tide you over until the next game.

While others are diving into open world games to sink hundreds upon hundreds of hours into them, you can rest assured that these games won’t eat up your schedule.

The thing about Outer Wilds is that the world itself is the final boss, with players only having a limited amount of time in order to save the universe – but it’s not done on its own. The game’s DLC, Echoes of the Eye, is about 10 and half hours long, obviously shorter for faster players.

The DLC doesn’t replace anything in the game, but it’s rather a separate and self-contained location, more than ready for players to dive in and unravel its secrets. This way, if players are wanting a taste of Outer Wilds without going through the whole game, they can easily do so.

This is especially the case if you’ve already beaten the game/solved the mystery of the main story. Since there isn’t really any replayability, the DLC offers a whole new mystery altogether – in a way, it’s like you’re playing the game for the first time all over again, and it can be solved pretty quickly.

Thankfully, there are also even more DLCs if you want more mystery, but they aren’t anywhere near as condensed as Echoes of the Eye.

There’s something particularly special about Shadow of the Colossus: the game is labelled as an open world, but many players would walk away from it thinking that it’s a semi-open world due to just how empty the world itself is.

Of course, that’s typically a bad thing for open worlds, but the unique thing about Shadow of the Colossus is that it would not work without that emptiness. Combine this with a linear order for the bosses themselves (which are platforming puzzles as well), a vague yet compelling story and a genuinely cool premise, and you’ve got a game that’s as fun as it is challenging.

One of my students refers to the game as “Rated T for Teen Mario,” and I'm bound to agree, if that helps get the idea across. And just like Mario, the game can be beaten pretty quickly: about 7 hours, in fact.

With that in mind, if this is a game that interests you, be prepared to spend most of those 7 hours climbing rather than fighting; you’re going to love it regardless.

Right now, The Legend of Zelda once again has the gaming community in a complete buzz thanks to the fantastic reception to the Ocarina of Time Remake.

The series is continuously revolutionary, constantly evolving and redefining the open world genre as we know it. However, many tend to forget that open world Zelda didn’t start with Breath of the Wild, it started with the very first entry in the entire franchise.

The nice part about the game is that it’s not long at all (especially when compared to its sequels that will come over the next few decades) – averaging only at about 8 hours to beat the game. Players who want a traditional Zelda experience in a short amount of time can’t find any other game that would be a better fit.

And as the game comes up on its 40th anniversary, it’s all the more reason to dive into where it all began.

Obviously, both Red Dead Redemption games are massive, telling all kinds of stories jam-packed in a rich world of historical fiction, so it would take a while to beat either entry. However, the first game’s DLC, Undead Nightmare, is a fantastic stand-alone story that only takes about 6 and a half hours to complete.

Undead Nightmare takes everything you love about the classic Red Dead Redemption, but with a twist: suddenly, everyone is trying to survive a zombie apocalypse that came about practically overnight. The world and everything you can do within it, naturally, is related to this instead of your standard robberies and bounties.

Since the world is so condensed, the DLC goes by much quicker than most, but it’s an absolute blast from start to finish. In fact, it’s widely considered to be one of the greatest DLCs of all time, simply for how refreshingly unique and fun it is.

With that in mind, the fact that this game can be completed quicker than a standard work shift just makes it all the better.

Of all the Assassin's Creed games, the shortest mainline entry (non-DLC game) is easily Assassin's Creed: Rogue, clocking in at about 11 hours to be beaten (again, it’s much quicker than that for veteran AC fans and seasoned gamers as a whole).

Surprisingly, the game has one of the more unique stories that the series has seen, focusing on an Assassin named Shay Patrick Cormac literally going rogue, slaughtering the brotherhood he knows and siding with the Templars.

And the best part of the story is the fact that the modern-day segments are thankfully incredibly short – the segments that drag and feel like a chore in all the other titles in the franchise don’t bog down this game.

Overall, it’s the perfect bite-sized game for Assassin’s Creed content, regardless of if you’re a fan or even brand new to the series. It’s truly one of a kind, especially for a series like AC.

From the titans of Xenoblade to the lawns of Santa Destroy, these Wii open-world games prove curiosity always pays off if you’re willing to get lost.

If you were given 10 hours to simply explore New York City and soak it all in, you wouldn’t even be an eighth of the way through your journey before you reach that time. The fact that Marvel's Spider-Man brought in NYC on a similar (still scaled down) scale cemented the game’s timeframe as you continue to whip around as The Friendly Neighborhood himself.

Yet, you don’t have anywhere near as many superhero duties in Spider-Man: Miles Morales, so obviously, it will take you a lot less time. It would take about 8 hours, in fact.

Since you’re playing the game as Miles Morales (duh) while Peter Parker is still around and kicking, you’re basically a superhero in training. This training will have you busy constantly taking down bad guys and saving the day, serving as the sole Spider-Man in NYC for several hours until Peter comes back from vacation with MJ.

Or you could just swing around New York City doing whatever you want for that timeframe, you’d get the same amount of enjoyment.

Just because a game is a horror game doesn’t mean it can’t also be open world, and in DREDGE, our open world is a vast, dangerous ocean. Even then, it’s nowhere near as dangerous as it will be once your sanity drains due to the Lovecraftian terrors you’ll encounter.

It sounds horrifying, but it’s actually the coziest fishing game you’d ever imagine. You fish, fill out your encyclopedia, discover aberrations with the marine life and upgrade your ship, but the real fun comes from the simplest mechanic: sorting the fish into your boat. Seriously, the inventory management is the most addictive part of the whole game.

The nice part is that it’s wrapped up quickly, too, taking only about 9 and a half hours to complete – but trust me, you’re going to willingly sink far more hours into the game (and your ship). And if that doesn’t sound like enough content in the game for how much I sing its praises, it also has two equally dense and fun DLCs.

When it comes to short, yet full open world games, you cannot get any better of an experience than with DREDGE.

The lovely thing about Eastshade isn’t just how stunning of a game it is, but also the fact that it can be beaten pretty quickly and pretty easily – just around 9 hours.

The whole game is about finding the most beautiful spots in the game to paint them (using a photography mechanic), so those entire 9 hours are filled with genuine beauty. Of course, since it’s open world, there are side quests (artwork commissions) and other things to do, but you’re going to be far more caught up in how pretty the world is.

And for those who love subtle, environmental storytelling, this world is full of it. You can learn more while you’re out and about exploring in it, or from the various other characters that you can talk to.

It’s one of the few open world games that keeps you busy without actively stressing you out; since, after all, the point of the game is to relax you, you’re going to find yourself in a comfortable state of bliss while playing.

If you’ve ever wanted to feel like you’re driving a pod around Tatooine (like any Star Wars fan would), you would have a fantastic time with Sable.

The game seems pretty surface-level and simple: just ride around on your sand-speeder and enjoy the game’s lovely art style, but once you start playing, you’ll see it’s a lot deeper than you’d expect. It’s supposed to be about the protagonist’s self-discovery on their home planet, but by the end of your adventure, you’re going to feel like you’ve gone on a self-discovery of your own.

While the game can be completed in about 7 and a half hours, it’s actually better if you take your time with the exploration – that’s the game’s strongest component, after all. Why not take the time to enjoy a world as pretty and interesting as this one?

It’s not perfectly polished; it’s actually pretty janky of a game at times, but if anything, it makes you love the game and all the charm it has even more. At the same time, if some of the previously mentioned jank (charm) is a little too much, then rest assured that you can get through this game very, very quickly.

A Short Hike is just that: short. It’s not the kind of short where it’s on the shorter end of a long game, no, the game is only about an hour and a half long. If you try to complete every single element within it to 100% the game, you’re looking at about 4 hours, an incredibly tiny open world game.

The premise of the game is simple: you’re hiking up a mountain. If you run into anyone or anything on the way there, you’re more than welcome to interact with them, but it’s optional if you’re wanting to just get to the top. Considering how short the game is, I’d recommend not skipping anything if you can help it, just to get the richest experience you can.

Don’t rush through this hike, either. The game is already short enough, and there is so much enjoyable content that you don’t want to miss out on while on the way to the top.

But as we’ve learned with games like these: it’s not about the destination, it’s about the journey, so don’t be afraid to go on that journey.

#4344. I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike

I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.

Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.

When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.

USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely new, but it’s surprisingly rare. Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the company’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model that’s slowly starting to ship.

The ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition. At €999, it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.

Of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.

And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.

Instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.

If I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.

Heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.

Plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.

The battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be quickly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.

I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.

It may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.

And that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.

Of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as quickly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.

But clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.

USB-C charging aside, there's a very good reason that just about every folding e-bike on the market has put thick plates on the folding connection of the frame. It's because the frame breaks if they're not there. Just like this one is going to.

I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road quickly.

But having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.

For years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.

Now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

#4343. Tesla Cybercab’s autonomy agreement is insane: $299/mo or it doesn’t move

Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.

And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the company started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

That personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

Then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps, and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.

Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.

Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.

Tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk said the cars were “the Model Ys we make currently, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027. The Cybercab launches on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.

So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.

Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.

Tesla’s answer to all those owners is a new car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.

I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.

You don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

There are three possible reasons Tesla isn't allowing model Y owners to use FSD in the allowed zones:

1: the robotaxis are in fact different from the model Ys being sold

2: Tesla doesn't have enough "remote operators" to cover all of those supposedly self-driving cars if users join the network

3: Tesla isn't willing to accept liability when FSD kills someone.

And the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no new revenue attached.

A new vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.

So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?

#4342. Stellantis Reappoints Broderdorf, Promotes Kuniskis in CEO Shuffle

Bob Broderdorf is returning from medical leave to lead Dodge, while Tim Kuniskis is taking over as Stellantis’s U.S. chief commercial officer.

Stellantis is playing another round of musical chairs with its executive team. This time, most of the changes stem from Bob Broderdorf’s return to the company. Broderdorf took medical leave from his position as Jeep’s CEO in August. He was replaced by Branden Coté, who retains his position as head of Jeep.

When Broderdorf’s departure from Jeep was announced, Stellantis had said he would come back in a different leadership role. Now off medical leave, Broderdorf will return to CEO status, this time as head of Dodge.

See all results for used cars for sale near 50317

This isn’t Broderdorf’s first time at Dodge. He’s held seven different positions related to marketing, sales, product planning, and operations throughout his 25-year tenure at Stellantis. Dodge has been led by Matt McAlear since 2024, but McAlear has been spread thin at Stellantis since February, when he took over as Chrysler’s CEO and head of Alfa Romeo North America. McAleer will now focus solely on Chrysler, which is expected to release three new models in the next few years.

Chrysler’s lineup currently consists of just the Pacifica minivan. However, the brand has already announced the Airflow, a new compact SUV slated to launch in 2028 and start at less than $40,000, and is also working on the Arrow and Arrow Cross, which will come in under $30,000.Both CEOs will report to Tim Kuniskis, who assumes a new role as U.S. chief commercial officer. Kuniskis joined Stellantis in 1992 and served in several leadership roles before retiring from his position as head of Dodge and Ram in May 2024.

Retirement only lasted about seven months, though, and Kuniskis reportedly said he was “bored to death” after about two weeks out of work. By December 2024, Stellantis had announced Kuniskis’s appointment as Ram’s CEO. Since his return, Kuniskis has passed the Ram brand to Matt VanDyke and has taken over as head of American Brands, North America Marketing, SRT, and Stellantis’s Direct Connection parts division.

Now, Kuniskis adds U.S. retail, fleet sales, and the dealer network to his long list of leadership divisions following the departure of Michael Orange, former senior vice president of U.S. sales and network performance. Kuniskis will report to Stellantis North America’s chief operating officer, Pablo Di Si, who was appointed to the role earlier this month.

See all results for used cars for sale near 50317

Di Si said in a press release that the leadership moves create a “clear line of decision-making” across the organization, which he says is important as Stellantis works to reach targets outlined in its FaSTLAne 2030 growth plan.

#4341. Huawei set to challenge Tesla Powerwall with new, 20 kW home battery

This high-tech Huawei home battery pack hopes to hold back Tesla’s latest Powerwall with silicon carbide technology, AI-powered energy management baked in, and enough modular storage to keep even large homes bright and warm when the rest of the block goes dark.

Huawei believes its new Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery. The Chinese tech firm is calling it an “all-in-one residential energy system” that combines a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, and AI-powered energy management in a single, simple, and stackable package that’s available in single-phase versions that put out between 3 and 10 kW and three-phase versions that can push up to 20 kW.

The Luterra S2 is the first system of its kind to use Huawei’s proprietary full-silicon carbide (SiC) architecture, which promises improved efficiency, power density, and ease of use. It’s so easy, in fact, that Huawei claims it can be installed and commissioned in just minutes.

“We are thrilled to introduce Huawei Luterra S2, our next-generation all-in-one residential energy system,” said Steve Zhang, President of Huawei Distributed PV & BESS Business. “By combining full-SiC architecture, AI-driven energy management, and industry-leading safety, Luterra S2 is designed to be smaller, lighter, quieter, safer, smarter and more powerful than ever before.”

Huawei’s basic Luterra S2 configuration starts with “just” 5 kWh of battery energy storage and 3 kW of output. That’s enough to keep essential household appliances, lighting, and electronics running during a power outage, but you’ll want to keep going if you’re preparing for more than a day or two without power.

If that sounds like you, Luterra’s got you covered. The modular system can be expanded with modular 7 kWh LFP battery packs and can scaling up to a massive 336 kWh of total storage across interconnected systems, with inverter output peaking at an impressive 60 kW using three 20 kW units in parallel.

Keeping all that power cool and quiet is a Huawei-developed passive cooling system that does without external fans, keeping operating noise levels below a claimed 29 dB (about the same as my Mac mini). It operates at ambient temperatures from –25° C to about 60° C, and features a sturdy IP66-rated enclosure (safe to hit with a high-pressure hose) with corrosion protection up to C5-M to keep it from rusting away.

Nice, but no mention of price or European availability.

Alas, the Luterra S2 probably won’t be making its way to the US anytime soon – but fear not! If you’re shopping for a Tesla Powerwall alternative that won’t help fund the absolute worst people in politics, there are a number of great home battery systems on the market that can deliver backup power, store your solar energy, and keep your home running when the grid goes down. #4340. Where Winds Meet December's calendar is full of new content, including a new region and the mobile launch you've been waiting for

You're probably nowhere near done with what's already in Where Winds Meet, but you better believe there's more on the way.

Where Winds Meet already has a staggering amount of content, but that’s not the end of what we can expect. Developer Everstone Studio just revealed a host of new additions coming to the game this month.

It’s clear that the developer is committed to the free-to-play action RPG, and the game’s recent success on Steam, and PlayStation has more than likely solidified the team’s plans for the future of the game.

On the official Where Winds Meet account on Twitter, the developer shared a brief roadmap of some of what we can expect over the course of December. The roadmap is split into the four weeks of the month, covering everything from smaller quests to more larger additions.

The first week started off a little light, with two new Jianghu Legacy Quests: Twelve Years of Feuds, and An Unholy Prophecy. Both quests are currently available in the game.

The biggest addition, of course, is the new Roarding Sands region, which becomes available the same day as the RPG’s global launch on mobile devices during the second week. Roarding Sands arrives December 11, along with a new campaign boss dubbed River Master.

Discover the Winds of December:🗺️New Region: Roaring Sands🌊New Bosses: River Master and Feng Ruzhi📱Global Mobile Launch: Dec 12 (UTC)🗡️New Hero's Realm, Sword Trial and more! pic.twitter.com/d12Ra9uXwb

We also expect a new boss, Feng Ruzhi, to be added to the game during the same week, as well as the arrival of the Velvet Shade Sect. Two limited-time activities kick off during the same week, too; The Fortune Beyond Parlor, and The Great Faceologist.

The third and fourth weeks of the month bring us the Scarlet Shock Sword Trial, as well as the new Blazing Gale Dance Hero’s Realm activity. Where Winds meet wraps it all up on December 30 with the Fireworks Festival.

#4339. 2028 Ford Mustang Cobra with a Race Car-Derived V-8 Is Worth Waiting For

The Cobra finally returns to the Mustang lineup and essentially resumes the track-focused role last held by the Shelby GT350.

Ford only just launched the Mustang Dark Horse SC earlier this year, but the Blue Oval brand isn’t letting up when it comes to high-performance versions of its iconic pony car. While the S650-generation Mustang introduced the new Dark Horse branding—at the expense of the legendary Shelby nameplate—and saw the arrival of the new $300,000-plus GTD, Ford’s upcoming Mustang variant revives a famous name from the past: Cobra. The new Mustang Cobra is expected to slot between the Dark Horse and Dark Horse SC as an indirect successor to the last Shelby GT350, providing track-ready performance and high-fidelity driver engagement.

The Shelby GT350, offered from 2015–2020, is considered one of the best Mustangs ever, thanks to its naturally aspirated flat-plane-crank 5.2-liter V-8 known as Voodoo. The last Cobra is also coveted by Mustang fans, so the new track-focused model has big shoes to fill. And with a new engine most likely under the Cobra’s hood, there’s potential for another legendary Mustang to be born.

See all results for new 2028 Ford Mustang for sale near 61938

The Cobra will continue to utilize the S650 platform, itself an evolution of the S550 chassis that underpinned the Mustang from 2015–2023. The Cobra will adapt the Mustang into a dedicated track car, and we think it will also spawn a more hardcore Cobra R with even more extreme aerodynamics, stronger brakes, and greater weight savings, potentially even removing the backseat. We expect the Cobra’s bodywork to be based on the Dark Horse SC, but with small tweaks and possibly a rear wing that harkens back to the 2000 Cobra R.

Mustang fans are obviously clamoring for the return of the Voodoo, but we don’t think that’s what Ford has in store. Fret not, however, because the automaker is cooking up something special for the new Cobra.

Instead of the 5.2-liter Voodoo, the new Cobra will pack a naturally aspirated 5.4-liter engine derived from the Mustang GT3 race car that has triumphed at the 24 Hours of Daytona and secured a podium at Le Mans. The Coyote-based GT3 engine features a cross-plane crank, but the teaser video released by Ford emitted a high-revving scream, so there’s a chance that the Cobra’s engine will switch to a flat-plane-crank setup. Still, if you’ve recently been to an IMSA race, you’ll know the GT3 car produces a thunderous soundtrack, so enthusiasts are in for an auditory treat regardless.

Although Ford hasn’t confirmed that the Cobra will adapt the GT3 race car’s engine, in the first teaser it said the car would pack a “heart born from racing.” We don’t expect the Cobra to come close to the Dark Horse SC or GTD in terms of power, but we wouldn’t be shocked if the 5.4-liter V-8 exceeds the 550 horsepower that the GT3 car is restricted to by racing regulations.

See all results for new 2028 Ford Mustang for sale near 61938

Better yet, the new 5.4-liter V-8 will be paired with a six-speed manual for maximum driver engagement. We think Ford will likely employ the Tremec TR-3160 transmission already used in the Dark Horse.

At the moment, the Mustang has the V-8 muscle car world all to itself. Dodge is expected to stuff a supercharged V-8 back into the Charger for the 2028 model year, while Chevy is gearing up to bring back the Camaro around 2028. The only other V-8-powered car under $100,000 is the Corvette, which has a completely different form factor with its mid-engine layout, but it will likely still be cross-shopped against the Cobra.

Pricing is probably the biggest risk. Ford needs to make sure it doesn’t alienate its customers by making it too expensive, given that the Dark Horse SC already has a hefty $105,585 asking price (about $20K more than the GT500 that it replaced). The new 5.4-liter V-8 will also have to make a strong impression as a successor to the much-loved Voodoo.

The Mustang Cobra will likely be revealed in early 2027 and go on sale before the end of the year. We expect pricing to start somewhere in the $80,000 range, but it could easily climb to $100,000 for a Cobra R model.

#4338. Check your ego at the door: Stellantis’ new electric dolly turns ANY car into a tow rig

We all know the type: grizzled stubble, wraparound PitVipers, a MAGA hat quietly retired after last week’s deep-blue shellacking, and a pristine, polished pickup parked in the driveway that they “need for towing.” With Stellantis’ new patent for an AI-powered electric tow dolly that turns just about ANY vehicle into a capable tow rig, however, those might need a new to find a new excuse to keep that gas-guzzler.

Originally filed in 2023, Stellantis received US Patent No. 12,779,916 for its electric tow dolly on 03NOV2026. The patent covers a machine that’s designed to shoulder the trailer’s hitch load with its own ball hitch or fifth-wheel plate, using an on-board electric motor and battery to get the trailer going while its regenerative braking system and AI-backed steering and traction control system keeps everything pointed in the right direction.

In other words, the dolly takes on many of the jobs that traditionally require a big tow vehicle: providing the pulling power, managing the trailer’s weight and controlling its braking and traction. The vehicle up front doesn’t necessarily need a massive motor, heavy-duty suspension or oversized brakes. With a system like this, you could argue that the “tow vehicle” isn’t really a tow vehicle at all. It’s more of a “lead vehicle,” since the dolly is the one doing the towing … and it can follow just about anything – including the diminutive (and supremely affordable) Fiat 500e, which is also made by Stellantis.

To be clear, this isn’t just Uncle Jojo making fun of the commuter conveys – Stellantis’ patent describes the dolly as being equipped with an autonomous control system using cameras, sensors, a controller, and an advanced, four wheel steer-by-wire system. It also specifically discusses how the dolly’s independently powered acceleration, braking and steering, and sway controls essentially remove the need to own a truck in the first place.

The dolly system’s truck bed sides and small size allow users to experience the functionality and utility of a truck only when they need it, allowing them to own a smaller, cheaper, and more fuel efficient vehicle that suits daily use needs.

There are some pretty obvious practical questions still to answer, of course, including how much battery capacity the dolly would need, how much weight it could handle and how it would perform on long grades or in emergency braking situations. And, to be clear, a patent isn’t a product announcement or proof that Stellantis plans to put one of these things on sale – heck, if I were Stellantis’ CEO, I’d patent this thing just to prevent anyone else from building one so I could keep selling ancient, low-tech, high-margin Ram Trucks – but it’s a neat idea.

Okay, I like this idea and appreciate the problem it is trying to solve, but it has the same challenge as any electric-tow situation, which is the charging logistics. Even if you find a pull-through charger (very rare), if you are using an EV, you still need to charge two "vehicles," so you have to charge your car, then pull up and charge the dolly afterwards. Even if you are using a gas car, charging the dolly will be logistically challenging. Of course, that's a problem with an easy solution (more pull-through chargers), but also one that doesn't seem to be on any charging network's radar.

I think it’s neat, anyway. What do you guys think? Are you ready to trade in your big-battery Chevy Silverado EV or Volvo VNR 800 on a new Topolino, or are you going to keep driving inefficient 99% of the time? Let us know, in the comments.

#4337. Battlefield 6's latest update dubbed the game's simultaneously best and worst patch as it runs into all kinds of issues

What's likely going to be the last major Battlefield 6 update of the year has launched with a number of unexpected issues.

There’s been a lot of anticipation for Battlefield 6’s version 1.1.3.0 patch. The patch kicks off the third and final phase of the game’s first season, adding some new holiday-themed content. More the new content itself, the update’s biggest additions are almost entirely gameplay-related.

Unfortunately, for as much as the changes in 1.1.3.0 have been well received, the launch has been marred by a series of technical issues, some of which are a little unusual.

Immediately after patch 1.1.3.0 went live, players on PC started reporting massive stutters that would occur every few seconds. The issue is especially pronounced in Redsec Battle Royale, but much deadlier in traditional multiplayer.

Battlefield Studios quickly acknowledged it, pointing out a workaround that appears to be working for players on Steam. According to those players, going offline on Steam’s friends menu has fixed stuttering for them.

The issue remains for other players on PC, however, and the developer said it’s working on a proper fix.

Perhaps the most disrupting problem the patch has caused is one that prevents players from being able to interact with the game’s menu. Tiles become unresponsive, or outright unselectable when you try to hover near them.

Ironically, the top set of tiles designed to make it easy for players to quickly jump into the new content has been the most affected. Restarting the game sometimes fixes the issue, and some players report that it only happens upon first launch after installing the update.

But Battlefield Studios later clarified that, unsurprisingly, there’s an actual reason behind the bug. Once again, a fix is being investigated, and the developer will offer an update once some progress has been made.

A little further down the list of importance is an issue that stops players from being able to skip tiers within the new Winter Offensive bonus path in the game’s battle pass. BF Studios took out the feature entirely while it works on a fix, so while you can continue making progress in the bonus path, you won’t be able to skip tiers.

This is all a shame to see. Outside of all the problems, the meat of the new update has been almost universally praised. The visibility improvements, and netcode updates have been celebrated. Many players were also happy to see meaningful updates to footstep audio and overall clarity.

It’s also unusual for a Battlefield 6 patch to run into so many issues at launch. The sentiment around 1.1.3.0 so far is that it’s the game’s best and worst update yet. Hopefully those issues will be fixed before the development team breaks for the holidays.

#4336. Treyarch Lays Off Call of Duty Zombies Mastermind Craig Houston After 20 Years

Contributor at DualShockers, former Esports Insider DACH content lead, former Escapist Magazine Germany content lead, software engineering background.

Craig Houston, the writer behind much of Call of Duty’s Zombies storyline, has been laid off by Treyarch after around 20 years at the studio.

As the development of Black Ops 7 winds down, Treyarch has indicated that they'll make big changes to Zombies in their future Call of Duty games.

He shared the news himself on Friday via X and LinkedIn, and I have to say, it’s a rather graceful message considering the circumstances. Houston said he was proud and privileged to have worked alongside so many talented people, many of whom will remain friends for life, before thanking fans for their enthusiasm, support and kind words over the years. On X, he posted it alongside a video celebrating 30 years of Treyarch, featuring footage from many of the games he worked on, which makes the whole thing feel a little more bittersweet.

He didn’t go into the reasons, but it appears to be part of the huge Xbox restructuring announced earlier this year, which is set to affect 3,200 jobs. Treyarch sits under Activision Blizzard, which in turn is owned by Xbox, so it isn’t a huge surprise that the cuts have reached the studio. Still, seeing a name like his on the list stings, especially if you’ve spent any amount of time shooting zombies with your friends at 2 in the morning.

For those who don’t know him by name, and I suspect that’s quite a few people, Houston has been at Treyarch since 2006. His first Call of Duty there was Call of Duty 3, where he worked as a video editor, which is a pretty humble start for someone who would go on to shape one of the series’ biggest modes. From World at War in 2008 onwards, he was the main writer for Zombies, whilst also writing for Treyarch’s campaigns.

He is credited as a writer and designer on Black Ops 1 through 4, and later as part of the design and creative development teams on the likes of Cold War, Black Ops 6 and Black Ops 7. Interestingly, he isn’t credited on this year’s Modern Warfare 4.

Zombies obviously wasn’t a one-man show, with Jimmy Zielinski, Jason Blundell and Kevin Drew all being a big part of how the mode evolved. Houston’s writing is what a lot of fans point to when they talk about why they fell in love with the characters, though. He also wrote the jingles for the original perks introduced in Verrückt, which is one of my favourite details in all of this. If you’ve ever caught yourself singing along to a vending machine whilst a horde closes in on you, that one’s on him.

The response since Friday has been lovely to see. Former Treyarch developer Tony Flame replied to Houston’s post calling him a legend and saying it was an honour to work with him, adding that he created a truly special experience that will live on for millions of fans. Over on Reddit, one fan described him as a great guy, noting that you can tell how much he loves the story and characters he writes simply by how excited he gets when talking about them in promo material.

Many fans argue that Houston never quite got the recognition he deserved. In the wake of this announcement, many people admitted they hadn’t really been aware of him until after Black Ops 3, despite him having been there since the very beginning, and I think that’s true for a lot of us players. We tend to know the directors and the faces from the trailers, whilst the people writing the lines we end up quoting for years stay in the background. Zombies a mode spawned out of passion, and it’s hard to see someone fundamentally involved with that leave.

Truth be told, this is the part of the Xbox restructuring that I find hardest to get my head around. Twenty years of knowing a story inside out, including every timeline, every character and every twist, isn’t something a studio can simply hire back in. Of course, I don’t know the reasoning behind this particular decision, and Houston himself hasn’t said a bad word about Treyarch. It is, however, a reminder that these layoff numbers are made up of people, some of whom have been shaping the games we love for the last two decades.

Houston hasn’t said what he plans to do next. Whatever it ends up being, I hope it involves writing, and ideally a jingle or two.
